This petition under Section 482 of Cr.P.C.is filed assailing the order dated 14.06.2024 passed in Cr.R. No. 81/2024 by the First Additional Sessions Judge, Ratlam whereby the order dated 13.03.2024 passed in Cr. Case No. 888/2023 by the Judicial Magistrate First Class, Ratlam was affirmed.

Learned Judicial Magistrate First Class declined to forward the complaint of petitioner for investigation u/s 156(3) of Cr.P.C.
2.

The exposition of facts, giving rise to the present petition, is as under:
A.

The petitioner has preferred an application against the respondents u/S 156(3) of Cr.P.C. interalia stating that the Office of District Women and Child Development Department published an advertisement in the daily newspaper on 20.10.2020 for o p e r a t i o n o f N E U T R A L C I T A T I O N N O . 2 0 2 6 : M P H C - I N D : 8 5 9 2 2 MCRC-40338-2024 Balika Grah and Swadhar Grah.

sentences.text: One Awsar Yuva Mandal Samiti submitted application in the prescribed format.
The petitioner came to know that the operation work of Balika Grah and Swadhar Grah has already been given to an Association, who had not applied for the operation work within the stipulated time.
The petitioner demanded list of all the desirous associations, who have applied for the operation work of Balika Grah and Swadhar Grah under the Right to Information Act.
It came to light from the information provided by the department that the Zahiruddin vs Ravindra Kumar Mishra on 1 April, 2026 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/87328631/
1 application filed by the petitioner has not been included in the said list.
Being aggrieved, the petitioner has preferred first appeal before the Collector.
The Collector vide order dated 30.06.2021 has decided the appeal and directed the District Programme Officer to give information within 15 days.
However, no information or documents have been provided to the petitioner.

The operation work of Balika Grah and Swadhar Grah was allotted to Nivedita Balika Grah Sanchalan Yuva Brigade Uthan Samiti, Ratlam by the Senior officials despite the application not being filed in the Form 27 within the stipulated time frame.

sentences.text: Sunil Puri and Sona Kushwah i.e. the respondents no. 3 & 4 in connivance the higher officials of the department got the operation work of Balika Grah and SwadharGrah in order to fulfill ulterior motive without following the due procedure prescribed by the State.
A complaint was filed by the petitioner before the Commissioner.
During inquiry on complaint, it was stated that no application has been filed by the petitioner.

However, the petitioner NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2026:MPHC-IND:8592 3 MCRC-40338-2024 has the acknowledgement of Inward Register, wherein the application of Yuva Mandal Samiti was received at Sr. No. 2161 dated 10.11.2020.

B. The Judicial Magistrate First Class, Ratlam after hearing the arguments had declined to forward the application under Sec. 156(3) for investigation and fixed the same for recording of evidence of complainant treating the application as a private complaint.
Feeling aggrieved by the order dated 13.03.2023 passed by the learned JMFC, a revision has been filed by the petitioner.
Learned Additional Sessions Judge dismissed the revision and affirmed the order of the Judicial Magistrate First Class.

3. Learned counsel for petitioner, in addition to the grounds mentioned in the petition submitted that the petitioner had filed an application u/S 156(3) of Cr.P.C., inter-alia requesting for forwarding the matter to the Police Station - Station Road, Ratlam to investigate into offence punishable u/S 420, 467, 468, 471, 201 and 120 B of IPC against accused, who are respondents in the present petition.

Learned Judicial Magistrate First Class, Ratlam declined to forward the complaint for investigation to the concerned police station despite constitution of cognizable offence from the contents of the complaint.
The learned counsel contended that learned Judicial Magistrate First Class, Ratlam did not apply judicial mind while declining to forward the complaint for investigation.
Learned Magistrate has erroneously opted to inquire into the complaint by the Court.
The order of learned JMFC is against the provisions of law.
Learned Revisional Court also committed NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2026:MPHC-IND:8592 4 MCRC-40338-2024 error in affirming the order of learned JMFC.
Learned counsel further submits that the investigation into the allegations of cognizable offence is necessary.
Therefore, the impugned order be set aside and the JMFC, Ratlam be directed to forward the complaint for investigation to the jurisdictional police station.
Learned counsel referred to the judgment passed in the case of Mukesh KharwarVs.
State of U.P. reported in (2024) 9 ILRA 457 to buttress his contentions.

4. Per contra, learned counsel appearing for respondent no. 1, 2 & 4 submitted that the learned JMFC had, in exercise of discretion, declined to forward the complaint for investigation for the reasons recorded in the order.

Learned counsel submitted that the matter requires verification of Zahiruddin vs Ravindra Kumar Mishra on 1 April, 2026 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/87328631/
2 certain facts by the Magistrate in view of previous communication between the parties.
Learned counsel further contended that the complainant did not report the matter to jurisdictional Police Station before filing of complaint and application u/S 156(3) of Cr.P.C.
Therefore, the mandate of law requiring the complainant to approach the police authorities first was not complied with.
There is no averment in the application that petitioner has approached the police authorities first.
No error is committed by the JMFC in declining to forward the complaint for investigation.
The petition is meritless and deserves to be dismissed.

In reply, learned counsel for the petitioner referring Annexure P-7 enclosed with his reply submitted that the petitioner had submitted a written complaint to the Superintendent of Police on 26.07.2022.
Thereafter, he had NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2026:MPHC-IND:8592 5 MCRC-40338-2024 filed a complaint on 22.10.2023.
Thus, there is substantial compliance with the mandate of law.

Learned counsel for the respondent pointed out that this application was submitted with the Office of Collector which is reflected from the acknowledgement seal.
5.
Heard learned counsel for both the parties and perused the record.
6. In the case of Mukesh Kharwar Vs. State of U.P. reported in (2024) 9 ILRA 457 also reported in 2024 SCC OnLine All 6035, learned single Judge of the Allahabad High Court held as under- 15.

sentences.text:
From the above discussion, it is clear that the scheme of Cr PC and the prevailing circumstances require that the option to direct the registration of the case and its investigation by the police should be exercised where some "investigation" is required, which is of a nature that is not possible for the private complainant, and which can only be done by the police upon whom statute has conferred the powers essential for investigation, for example:
(1) where the full details of the accused are not known to the complainant and the same can be determined only as a result of investigation, or (2) where recovery of abducted person or stolen property is required to be made by conducting raids or searches of suspected places or persons, or (3) where for the purpose of launching a successful prosecution of the accused evidence is required to be collected and preserved.

To illustrate by example cases may be visualised where for production before Court at the trial (a) sample of blood soaked soil is to be taken and kept sealed for fixing the place of incident; or (b) recovery of case property is to be made and kept sealed; or (c) recovery under Section 27 of the Evidence Act; or (d) preparation of inquest report; or (e) witnesses are not known and have to be found out or discovered through the process of investigation 16.

Thus, where the complainant is in possession of the complete details of all the accused as well as the witnesses who have to be examined and neither recovery is needed nor any such material evidence is required to be collected which can be done only by the police, no "investigation" would normally be required and the procedure of complaint case should be adopted.

It must be kept in Zahiruddin vs Ravindra Kumar Mishra on 1 April, 2026 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/87328631/
3 mind that adding unnecessary cases to the diary of the police would impair their efficiency in respect NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2026:MPHC-IND:8592 6 MCRC-40338-2024 of cases genuinely requiring investigation
Besides even after taking cognizance and proceeding under Chapter XV the Magistrate can still under Section 202(1) Cr. P.C. order investigation, even thought of a limited nature.

17. The position has been clarified in the judgment passed by the Apex Court in the case of Suresh Chand Jain v. State of M.P. , (2001) 2 SCC 628 which while dealing with the issue has held as follows:--
"Any Judicial Magistrate, before taking cognizance of the offence, can order investigation under Section 156(3) of the Code.

entities.text: Suresh Chand Jain v. State of M.P. , (2001) 2 SCC 628
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: If he does so, he is not to examine the complainant on oath because he was not taking cognizance of any offence therein.
For the purpose of enabling the police to start investigation, it is open to the Magistrate to direct the police to register an FIR there is nothing illegal in doing so.

After all registration of an FIR involves only the process of entering the substance of the information relating to the commission of the cognizable offence in a hook kept by the officer in charge of the police station as indicated in Section 154 of the Code

Even if a Magistrate does not say in so many words while directing investigation under Section 156(3) of the Code that an FIR should be registered, it is the duty of the officer in charge of the police station to register the FIR regarding the cognizable offence disclosed by the complaint because that police officer could take further steps contemplated in Chapter XII of the Code only thereafter."

19. Perusal of the impugned order shows that no sufficient reason has been disclosed, on the basis of which, the Magistrate has proceeded to treat the application under section 156(3) Cr. P.C. as a complaint.
Merely because the facts are in the knowledge of the applicant, direction to lodge FIR cannot be refused.

The gravity/seriousness of the offence; the requirement of the evidence for the purpose of launching a successful prosecution, and basically the interest of justice depending on the facts of each case, need be considered in passing the order under Section 156(3) Cr. P.C.

The impugned order does not assign any valid reason nor reflects application of judicious mind and has been passed in a mechanical manner only on the ground that the facts of the case were within the knowledge of the applicant, thus, the same is liable to be set-aside.

7. The Apex Court in the case of Ramdev Food Products (P) Ltd. v. State of Gujarat, reported in (2015) 6 SCC 439 has observed as under :
6.

entities.label: PRECEDENT

However, in the light of submissions made during the hearing, we frame the following questions for consideration:
6.1. (i) Whether discretion of the Magistrate to call for a report under Section 202 instead of directing investigation under Section 156(3) is controlled by any defined parameters?

4 6.2 (ii) ................................

(iii) Whether in the present case, the Magistrate erred in seeking report under Section 202 instead of directing investigation under Section 156(3)?
It has been held, for the same reasons, that direction by the Magistrate for investigation under Section 156(3) cannot be given mechanically.

In Anil Kumar v. M.K. Aiyappa (2013) 10 SCC 705 :
(2014) 1 SCC (Cri) 35, it was observed :
11.

(2014) 1 SCC (Cri) 35
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: "The scope of Section 156(3) CrPC came up for consideration before this Court in several cases.

This Court in Maksud Saiyed case [Maksud Saiyed v. State of Gujarat,
(2008) 5 SCC 668 : (2008) 2 SCC (Cri) 692] examined the requirement of the application of mind by the Magistrate before exercising jurisdiction under Section 156(3) and held that where jurisdiction is exercised on a complaint filed in terms of Section 156(3) or Section 200 CrPC, the Magistrate is required to apply his mind

entities.text:
Maksud Saiyed v. State of Gujarat,
(2008) 5 SCC 668 : (2008) 2 SCC (Cri) 692
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: , in such a case, the Special Judge/Magistrate cannot refer the matter under Section 156(3) against a public servant without a valid sanction order.
The application of mind by the Magistrate should be reflected in the order.
The mere statement that he has gone through the complaint, documents and heard the complainant, as such, as reflected in the order, will not be sufficient.

After going through the complaint,
documents and hearing the complainant, what weighed with the Magistrate to order investigation under Section 156(3) CrPC, should be reflected in the order, though a detailed expression of his views is neither required nor warranted.
We have already extracted the order passed by the learned Special Judge which, in our view, has stated no reasons for ordering investigation."

The above observations apply to category of cases mentioned in para 120.6 in Lalita Lalita Kumari v.
State of U.P., (2014) 2 SCC 1.
21.

entities.text:
Lalita Lalita Kumari v.
State of U.P., (2014) 2 SCC 1
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: On the other hand, power under Section 202 is of different nature.
Report sought under the said provision has limited purpose of deciding "whether or not there is sufficient ground for proceeding".
If this be the object, the procedure under Section 157 or Section 173 is not intended to be followed.

Section 157 requires sending of report by the police that the police officer suspected commission of offence from information received by the police and thereafter the police is required to proceed to the spot, investigate the facts and take measures for discovery and arrest.
Thereafter, the police has to record statements and report on which the Magistrate may proceed under Section 190.
This procedure is applicable when the police receives information of a cognizable offence, registers a case and forms the requisite opinion and not every case registered by the police.

22. Thus, we answer the first question by holding that:
22.1.
The direction under Section 156(3) is to be issued, only after application of mind by the Magistrate.

When the Magistrate does not take cognizance and does not find it Zahiruddin vs Ravindra Kumar Mishra on 1 April, 2026 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/87328631/
5 necessary to postpone the issuance of process and finds a case made out to proceed forthwith
, direction under the said provision is issued.

In other words, where on account of credibility of information available, or weighing the interest of NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2026:MPHC-IND:8592 8 MCRC-40338-2024 justice it is considered appropriate to straightaway direct investigation, such a direction is issued.
22.2. The cases where Magistrate takes cognizance and postpones issuance of process are cases where the Magistrate has yet to determine "existence of sufficient ground to proceed".

Category of cases falling under para 120.6 in Lalita Kumari may fall under Section 202.
22.3.

Subject to these broad guidelines available from the scheme of the Code,
exercise of discretion by the Magistrate is guided by interest of justice from case to case.
We now come to the last question whether in the present case the Magistrate ought to have proceeded under Section 156(3) instead of Section 202.
Our answer is in the negative.
The Magistrate has given reasons, which have been upheld by the High Court.
The case has been held to be primarily of civil nature.
The accused is alleged to have forged partnership.
Whether such forgery actually took place, whether it caused any loss to the complainant and whether there is the requisite mens-rea are the questions which are yet to be determined.
The Magistrate has not found clear material to proceed against the accused.
Even a case for summoning has not yet been found.

While a transaction giving rise to cause of action for a civil action may also involve a crime in which case resort to criminal proceedings may be justified, there is judicially acknowledged tendency in the commercial world to give colour of a criminal case to a purely commercial transaction.
This Court has cautioned against such abuse.
8. In case of Rameshbhai Pandurao Hedau v. State of Gujarat, reported in (2010) 4 SCC 185, it was observed that - 25.

entities.text: Rameshbhai Pandurao Hedau v. State of Gujarat, reported in (2010) 4 SCC 185
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: The power to direct an investigation to the police authorities is available to the Magistrate both under Section 156(3) CrPC and under Section 202 CrPC.
The only difference is the stage at which the said powers may be invoked.

As indicated hereinbefore, the power under Section 156(3) CrPC to direct an investigation by the police authorities is at the pre-cognizance stage while the power to direct a similar investigation under Section 202 is at the post-cognizance stage.

26. The learned Magistrate has chosen to adopt the latter course and has treated the protest petition filed by the appellant as a complaint under Section 200 of the Code and has thereafter proceeded under Section 202 CrPC and kept the matter with himself for an inquiry in the facts of the case.

There is nothing irregular in the manner in which the learned Magistrate has proceeded and if at the stage of sub section (2) of Section 202 the learned Magistrate deems it fit, he may either dismiss the complaint under Section 203 or proceed in terms of Section 193 and commit the case to the Court of Session.

Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/87328631/
6 9.

Recently, in case of Om Prakash Ambadkar v. State of Maharashtra, NEUTRAL CITATION NO.
2026:MPHC-IND:8592 9 MCRC-40338-2024 reported in (2026) 2 SCC 622, it was held that - 26.

entities.text:
Om Prakash Ambadkar v. State of Maharashtra, NEUTRAL CITATION NO.
2026:MPHC-IND:8592 9 MCRC-40338-2024 reported in (2026) 2 SCC 622
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: It is, thus, not necessary that in every case where a complaint has been filed under Section 200CrPC the Magistrate should direct the police to investigate the crime merely because an application has also been filed under Section 156(3)CrPC even though the evidence to be led by the complainant is in his possession or can be produced by summoning witnesses, with the assistance of the court or otherwise.
The issue of jurisdiction also becomes important at that stage and cannot be ignored.

27. In fact, the Magistrate ought to direct investigation by the police only where the assistance of the investigating agency is necessary and the court feels that the cause of justice is likely to suffer in the absence of investigation by the police.

The Magistrate is not expected to mechanically direct investigation by the police without first examining whether in the facts and circumstances of the case, investigation by the State machinery is required or not.

If the allegations made in the complaint are simple, where the court can straightaway proceed to conduct the trial, the Magistrate is expected to record evidence and proceed further in the matterinstead of passing the buck to the police under Section 156(3)CrPC.

Of course, if the allegations made in the complaint require complex and complicated investigation which cannot be undertaken without active assistance and expertise of the State machinery, it would only be appropriate for the Magistrate to direct investigation by the police authorities.
The Magistrate is, therefore, not supposed to act merely as a post office and needs to adopt a judicial approach while considering an application seeking investigation by the police.
10. The material on record is examined in light of aforestated propositions of law.
11. Apparently, the petitioner was aggrieved by the grant of operation work of Balika Grah and Swadhar Grah to the respondent no. 3 and 4.
He complained and alleged violation of Rules and due procedure prescribed by the State.

As reflected from para 9 of the Order dated 14.06.2024 of the Revisional Court, the complaint was filed, as baseless by concerned authority and no cognizable offence was reported in the preliminary enquiry report submitted by Police Station, Station Road,
Ratlam.
Learned Judicial Magistrate First Class did not rely on the report.

Rather, the Judicial Magistrate has exercised his discretion to proceed under Section 200 of the NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2026:MPHC-IND:8592 10 MCRC-40338-2024 Cr.P.C and granted opportunity to complainant examine himself and witnesses.
The exercise of discretion and conclusion of learned Judicial Magistrate First Class, Ujjain cannot be said to be manifestly improper or illegal.
The Revisional Court committed no error in affirming the order of learned Judicial Magistrate First Class.

Therefore, no case is made out for interference in exercise of inherent jurisdiction under Section 482 of Cr.P.C.
12.
